title: Shuffle String
statement: You get a string `s` and an integer array `indices` with one entry per character of `s`. Build a new string of the same length in which the character `s[i]` lands at position `indices[i]`, for every `i`, and return it. The values of `indices` are distinct and each is a valid position, so every position receives exactly one character.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
all values of indices are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

Each character already knows where it belongs: `indices[i]` is its destination. So there is nothing to search for; write every character straight into its slot of an output buffer, then read the buffer from left to right. Looking up, for each output position, which character goes there would also work, but that search costs O(n²).

## Approach

1. Make `result`, an array with `n` empty slots, one per character of `s`.
2. For each `i`, read its destination `target = indices[i]` and write `s[i]` into `result[target]`.
3. Join `result` into a string and return it. Because `indices` is a permutation, every slot is filled exactly once.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "codeleet"`, `indices = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 2, 1, 3]`. `c`, `o`, `d`, `e` go to slots 4, 5, 6, 7; then `l` goes to 0, `e` to 2, `e` to 1 and `t` to 3. Reading slots 0 to 7 gives `l e e t c o d e`, so the answer is `"leetcode"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one write per character and one join.
- Space: O(n) for `result`.

## Pitfalls

- The direction matters: it is `result[indices[i]] = s[i]`, not `result[i] = s[indices[i]]`; the second applies the inverse permutation and only happens to work when the permutation is its own inverse.
- Strings in JavaScript are immutable, so assigning into a string index does nothing; fill an array and join it.
- Building the answer by repeated string concatenation in a fixed order does not work, because slots are filled out of order.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `s` (and of `indices`) |
| `result` | output buffer; slot `p` holds the character sent to position `p` |
| `i` | index of the current character in `s` |
| `target` | destination of `s[i]`, which is `indices[i]` |

narration.2: Both inputs have n entries, one per character.
narration.3: Make an output buffer with one slot per character.
narration.4: Visit every character of s once.
narration.5: Look up where the character at index i must go.
narration.6: Write it straight into that slot; distinct indices mean no slot is written twice.
narration.8: Every slot is now filled; join them into the shuffled string.
